latin.547: §. XII. Ceterum OCTAVUM SECULUM, quod unà cum Septimo, divinæ iræ Seculum rectissimè appellitat prædictus Mejerus, initio Sectionis suæ nonæ p. 177, Uti Imaginum in templis & oratoriis sacris defensione, ita & veritatis Eucharisticæ in falsitatem, id est, panis & vini, in Corporis & Sanguinis Christi, immutatione, utrâque argumentis rationi falsæ & Sapientiæ humanæ unicè debitis, innixâ, quin multis præterea, tam in Doctrina, quàm in ritibus, sapientium sibi visorum mortalium inventis commentisque, famosum est (Quo de videatur Spanhemius noster, Hist. Imag. Sect. I. §. XI. p. 33.)
latin.548: adeo, ut Christianæ istius Seculi Ecclesiæ, ex majori sui parte consideratæ, applicari illud debeat, quod Paulus de Ethnicis ad Romanos scribit: Proptereà, quòd cùm Deum noverint, tamen ut Deum non glorificaverunt, sed vani facti sunt in ratiocinationibus suis & obtenebratum est Cor eorum, intelligentiâ carens, cùm se dictitant Sapientes, stulti facti sunt & mutarunt gloriam DEI incorruptibilis in efformatas omnis generis imagines panisque spumam, olim à posteris suis adorandam.
latin.549: Certe ipse Johannes Damascenus, illius Seculi, præ ceteris, Doctor Celebratissimus, deque Orthodoxia, in suis de ea libris quatuor, ad hodiernorum, Orthodoxiæ monopolium sibi vindicantium, gloriatus modum, uti pro imaginibus scribendo decertavit acriter (annotantibus id Chronologis Celeberrimis, Calvisio & Helviso ad annum Christi 728. & 730., paginis mihi 625. & 112.) ita ad Pontificios de Eucharistia sentiendi loquendique modos erroneos divertit, seu potius hisce prælusisse censendus est, quando de fide Orthodoxa lib. 4. cap. 4. ita scribit: Quemadmodum naturaliter panis per commestionem, & vinum atque aqua, per bibitionem, in corpus & sanguinem edentis & bibentis commutantur & aliud fiunt corpus, præter prius illud corpus; Sic panis & vinum & aqua propositionis, per invocationem & adventum Sancti Spiritûs, supernaturaliter COMMUTANTUR in corpus & sanguinem Christi, à Theophylacto idcirco emendandus, notante Wittakero, pag. 102.
latin.550: aliarum quoque plurimarum innovationum & Terminorum, scholasticorum deinceps dictorum, temerè satis sanctæ Religioni & Theologiæ Christianæ intrusorum reus, quin Autor postulatus à sæpius laudato Mejero, paragraphum tertium Sectionis suæ octavæ ita exorso: Capita prætereà hôc seculo nova ratio tractandi doctrinam religionis Christianæ, auctore Damasceno, qui eam, ad modum scientiæ, primus tradere instituit. Hic, omissis quibusdam momentosis articulis, spinosas & inutiles quæstiones in Theologiam intulit, novas doctorum opiniones, ut religionis Christianæ dogmata proposuit, rarius ad Scripturam provocavit; formam sanorum verborum neglexit, formulis philosophorum potiùs, quam theologorum antiquorum & scripturæ utens. Et quia plerique postsecuti Doctores istam tractandi rationem sunt amplexi, sensim simplex veterum de religione Christianâ doctrinæ ratio, mutata est in scholasticas disputationes. p. 174. & 175.
latin.551: Intereà deviantibus ita à veritate multijuga, Damasceno & asseclis quàm plurimis, eodem seculo Octavo, errorum flumini, universam Ecclesiam inundaturo, sese opposuere verè Orthodoxi, i. e. Scripturæ S. pressius inhærentes haud pauci, dum sedibus suis undique exciti, Constantinopolim convenerunt Concilium, ab hac Civitate denominatum quintum, Græcis Oecumenicum septimum dictum, sub Constant. Copronymo & Leone Isaurico, à varia fama & æstimationis suæ proterva laceratione per Spanhemium nostrum vindicatis, celebratum; Hi per FIGURAM CORPORIS CHRISTI quam in Cœna statuebant, omnem figurarum seu Imaginum omnium usum sacrum abrogare éque medio tollere conabantur,
latin.552: eo tamen nomine passuri contradictionem gravissimam, sub pessimâ Irene, ab Iconolatris Nicænis, qui panem, in S. Cœna, non Figuram Corporis, sed ipsum corpus Christi, per Conversionem esse, acerrimè contendebant, id quod fusiùs Annotat. 3. §. 3. indicavimus.

pass_a.547: §. XII. For the rest, the EIGHTH AGE, which together with the Seventh the aforesaid Mejerus most rightly calls an Age of divine wrath, at the beginning of his ninth Section p. 177, is infamous both by the defense of Images in temples and sacred oratories and by the mutation of Eucharistic truth into falsehood — that is, of bread and wine into the Body and Blood of Christ — each resting on arguments owed solely to false reason and human Wisdom, and moreover by many inventions and fictions of mortals who seemed wise to themselves, both in Doctrine and in rites (on which see our Spanheim, Hist. Imag. Sect. I. §. XI. p. 33).
pass_a.548: so much so that to the Christian Church of that Age, considered for the greater part, there ought to be applied what Paul writes concerning the Gentiles to the Romans: Because although they knew God, yet they did not glorify Him as God, but became vain in their reasonings and their Heart was darkened, lacking understanding; when they call themselves Wise, they became fools and changed the glory of the incorruptible GOD into fashioned images of every kind and the foam of bread, someday to be adored by their posterity.
pass_a.549: Certainly John of Damascus himself, that Age’s Doctor most Celebrated above the rest, and concerning Orthodoxy in his four books on it glorying after the fashion of today’s claimants of Orthodoxy’s monopoly — just as he fought sharply in writing for images (the most Celebrated Chronologists Calvisius and Helvisus noting this at the years of Christ 728 and 730, pages to me 625 and 112), so he turned aside to the Pontificals’ erroneous modes of sensing and speaking about the Eucharist, or rather is to be judged to have prelude-played them, when in On the Orthodox Faith Book 4 ch. 4 he writes thus: Just as naturally bread by eating, and wine and water by drinking, are changed into the body and blood of the eater and drinker and become another body besides that prior body; So the bread and wine and water of the proposition, by the invocation and coming of the Holy Spirit, are supernaturaliter CHANGED into the body and blood of Christ — therefore to be emended by Theophylact, Whittaker noting, p. 102.
pass_a.550: He is also guilty of very many other innovations and Terms afterward called scholastic, rashly enough thrust into sacred Religion and Christian Theology — nay, postulated as Author by the often-praised Mejerus, who begins the third paragraph of his eighth Section thus: Moreover in this age there takes head a new way of treating the doctrine of the Christian religion, with Damascene as author, who first instituted to hand it down after the manner of a science. He, omitting certain momentous articles, brought thorny and useless questions into Theology, proposed new opinions of doctors as dogmas of the Christian religion, more rarely appealed to Scripture; neglected the form of sound words, using formulas of philosophers rather than of ancient theologians and of scripture. And because most Doctors who followed afterward embraced that way of treating, gradually the simple manner of the ancients’ doctrine concerning the Christian religion was changed into scholastic disputations (pp. 174 and 175).
pass_a.551: Meanwhile, Damascene and very many followers thus wandering from the manifold truth, in the same Eighth age not a few truly Orthodox — i.e. those clinging more closely to Holy Scripture — opposed themselves to the flood of errors about to inundate the universal Church, when stirred from their seats on every side they gathered at Constantinople a Council called from this City the fifth, by the Greeks said to be the seventh Oecumenical, under Constantine Copronymus and Leo the Isaurian, vindicated by our Spanheim from varied fame and the wanton laceration of their reputation; These, by the FIGURE OF CHRIST’S BODY which they set in the Supper, were trying to abrogate and remove from the midst every sacred use of figures or of all Images,
pass_a.552: yet on that account about to suffer the heaviest contradiction, under the worst Irene, from the Nicaean Iconolaters, who most sharply contended that the bread in the Sacred Supper is not the Figure of the Body but the body of Christ itself by Conversion — which we indicated more fully in Annotat. 3 §. 3.

547: §.XII: the EIGHTH age — with the Seventh, Mejerus’s age of divine wrath — is infamous for defending images in temples and for mutating Eucharistic truth into falsehood.
Bread and wine into Body and Blood, each propped on false reason and human wisdom, plus many mortal inventions in doctrine and rites (Spanheim, Hist. Imag.).
548: So far that Paul’s charge against the Gentiles (Romans) fits most of this age’s Christian Church:

Knowing God they did not glorify Him; claiming to be wise they became fools and exchanged the glory of the incorruptible God for fashioned images of every kind — and the foam of bread for posterity to adore.
549: John of Damascus, that age’s chief Doctor of Orthodoxy, fought sharply for images (Calvisius/Helvisus note ~728–730) — and turned toward (or rather preluded) Pontifical errors on the Eucharist.

Orthodox Faith 4.4: as bread and wine naturally change into the eater’s body, so the bread, wine, and water of the proposition are supernaturally CHANGED into Christ’s body and blood — Theophylact must emend him (Whittaker).
550: Guilty also of many later ‘scholastic’ terms rashly thrust into sacred theology — Mejerus names Damascene author of a new scientific method of treating Christian doctrine.

Thorny useless questions; new opinions as dogmas; rare appeal to Scripture; philosopher-formulas over sound words — and followers gradually turned the ancients’ simple doctrine into scholastic disputations.
551: Meanwhile truly Orthodox (Scripture-clinging) opposed Damascene’s flood of errors in the same Eighth age.

Gathered at Constantinople (fifth / Greeks’ seventh Oecumenical; Copronymus and Leo Isaurian — Spanheim vindicates them): by the FIGURE OF CHRIST’S BODY they set in the Supper they tried to abolish every sacred use of images.
552: Under worst Irene they met heaviest contradiction from Nicaean Iconolaters, who contend the Supper bread is not the Figure of the Body but Christ’s body itself by Conversion (see Annotat. 3 §.3).
Stop before §.XIII (ninth century; Charlemagne / Bertram reclaiming).
